questions.enonce_markdown:
Outline:

(i) Mendel's First Law of inheritance.

(ii) Mendel's Second Law of inheritance. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Mendel's First Law (the law of segregation).** Each characteristic of an organism is controlled by a **pair of factors (alleles, one from each parent)**. During the formation of gametes (meiosis) the **two alleles of a pair separate (segregate)**, so that **each gamete receives only one allele of each pair**. The alleles come together again at random at fertilisation. Example: a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes $Tt \times Tt$ gives a $3:1$ phenotypic ratio ($1\,TT : 2\,Tt : 1\,tt$) in the offspring.

**(ii) Mendel's Second Law (the law of independent assortment).** When **two or more pairs of contrasting characteristics** are followed together, the **alleles of different genes assort independently of one another into the gametes**: the separation of one pair of alleles has no effect on the separation of another pair. A dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes ($AaBb \times AaBb$) therefore gives four types of gametes in equal numbers and a **$9:3:3:1$** ratio in the offspring. (The law holds only for genes on **different chromosomes**; genes on the same chromosome are linked.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain, using appropriate genetic symbols, the possible blood groups of children whose father is heterozygote blood group A and mother heterozygote blood group B. *[14 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The ABO blood group system** is controlled by one gene with **three alleles** (multiple alleles): $I^A$ (makes antigen A), $I^B$ (makes antigen B) and $i$ (makes no antigen). $I^A$ and $I^B$ are **codominant** with each other and both are **dominant over $i$**.

| Phenotype (group) | Possible genotypes |
|---|---|
| A | $I^A I^A$ or $I^A i$ |
| B | $I^B I^B$ or $I^B i$ |
| AB | $I^A I^B$ |
| O | $ii$ |

**Parents.** A heterozygous group A father is $I^A i$; a heterozygous group B mother is $I^B i$.

| | |
|---|---|
| Parental phenotypes | Group A father $\times$ Group B mother |
| Parental genotypes | $I^A i$ $\times$ $I^B i$ |
| Gametes (meiosis) | $I^A$ or $i$ (father) ; $I^B$ or $i$ (mother) |

**Fertilisation (Punnett square, random fusion of gametes)**

| | $I^B$ | $i$ |
|---|---|---|
| **$I^A$** | $I^A I^B$ | $I^A i$ |
| **$i$** | $I^B i$ | $ii$ |

**Offspring**

| Genotype | Phenotype (blood group) | Proportion |
|---|---|---|
| $I^A I^B$ | AB | 1/4 |
| $I^A i$ | A | 1/4 |
| $I^B i$ | B | 1/4 |
| $ii$ | O | 1/4 |

**Conclusion.** The children of these parents can have **any one of the four blood groups, A, B, AB or O**, in the ratio **$1 : 1 : 1 : 1$**; each child has a 1 in 4 chance of each group. The group AB shows codominance (both alleles are expressed) and group O appears because both parents carry the recessive allele $i$.

questions.enonce_markdown: If these parents have two children, what is the probability that both will have blood group A? *[2 marks]* *(4, 14, 2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
From (b), the probability that **one child** has group A ($I^A i$) is **1/4**.

The two births are **independent events**, so the probabilities are multiplied (product rule):

$$P(\text{both group A}) = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{16}$$

**Probability = 1/16 (0.0625, or 6.25 per cent).**
